So, in a sense, the best way to explore what other habitable worlds might look like is to understand more about our own. That’s what researchers set out to do in a new study that simulated what Earth would look like if life never developed. Their findings, published in The Planetary Science Journal and flagged by ScienceAlert , could help astronomers distinguish which atmospheric signatures they see on other worlds can be independent of life — and which ones can only be explained by its presence. “When we interpret observations of an exoplanet’s atmosphere, this tool will help us determine the probability that what we observe indicates life on the surface,” said lead author Samantha Gilbert-Janizek, an astronomer at UC Riverside, in a statement about the work. The research, crucially, also explores whether our planet would still maintain its habitability without life ever intervening. In the study, the researchers built a computer model based on the planet’s geochemical systems, using physical factors like the properties of its core, the movement of its crusts and its oceans, and how it would all affect the exchange of chemicals between the core up to the surface of the planet and atmosphere. In all, they incorporated 19 different non-biological properties of a rocky planet and used it to simulate how Earth evolved over five billion years. Perhaps not so flatteringly to lifeforms, the Earth didn’t change too much without us around and stayed more than habitable. The oceans still held a similar amount of water, and surface temperatures stayed well within a comfortable range. candidates.title: People Who Got Hormone Therapy as Teenagers End Up With a Lower Regret Rate Years Later Than Knee Replacement Surgery, Research Finds
candidates.raw_excerpt: One of the most pernicious lines of attacks used to denigrate transgender people has been “transition regret” — the notion that a significant number of patients who undergo gender affirming treatment will go on to feel badly about the process. But new research finds that hormone therapy, one of the most common treatments in trans medicine, has a phenomenally low rate of regret — lower, in fact, than common procedures like knee replacement surgery. According to the study, published in JAMA Pediatrics and reported by the Washington Post , the vast majority of patients who undergo hormone replacement therapy (HRT) as teenagers have no regrets years later. To reach that conclusion, researchers followed 372 transgender and gender-diverse people who chose to go through with hormone therapy. The average participant was around 16 when they began hormone therapy, and around 21 when the survey results were collected. The numbers are stark: of those who do undergo HRT, nearly 97 percent of participants affirmed it was the right choice five years later. Just 2.7 percent said they regretted the therapy, which included seven who said the treatment harmed them. For context, that’s a lower dissatisfaction rate than common orthopedic procedures like knee replacement surgery, which has a regret rate ranging between 10 and 20 percent , depending on what data you examine. The satisfaction rate for hormone replacement is slightly higher than even the rosiest findings around hip replacement, where only around five percent of patients express regret. Though less than 0.1 percent of youth in the US will ever undergo HRT, the findings support past research which found that gender affirming care is an overwhelming net benefit for trans youth — contrary to the messaging from right-wing politicians who hone in on the regrets of a handful of vocal detransitioners. candidates.raw_excerpt: A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times. Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars . Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year. On June 14, as it headed towards perihelion – the closest point in its orbit to the sun, at a distance from our star of 1.5 times the distance between the Earth and the sun (known as an astronomical unit) , 220P suddenly and without warning burst into life. On 31 May, the comet was languishing at magnitude +17.39 (the higher the magnitude, the fainter an object is), but within less than 14 hours it had dramatically brightened to magnitude +11.05, bringing it into range for observation with small amateur telescopes. By June 2, 220P was up to magnitude +8.23 and was technically visible for a short while in 10x50 binoculars from a dark site, prompting amateur astronomers and astrophotographers to chase down this rare event. By perihelion, the comet had faded back to magnitude +12, but more was to come. A second outburst began at the end of July, brightening from magnitude +14 on 28 July to magnitude 6.1 by 6 August. candidates.title: IEA Chief hails China's role in supporting global energy transition
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Energy transition has become a major focus for delegates at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31). In an interview with China Media Group (CMG), International Energy Agency (IEA) Executive Director Fatih Birol said balancing energy security with the green transition is a common challenge worldwide, noting that China's clean-energy development and advances in green industries will help more countries advance their low-carbon transitions.

Birol said intensifying geopolitical conflicts are prompting countries to speed up their energy transitions, which are not only about tackling climate change but are also closely tied to energy security and economic development.

SpaceX's Starship spacecraft returned to its launch site on Saturday and was successfully caught by the launch tower's giant mechanical arms for the first time, marking a major milestone in the company's efforts to develop a fully reusable rocket system.

The giant rocket lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase facility in the US state of Texas on Friday afternoon. After more than 22 hours in space, it returned to the launch site on Saturday, completing Starship's 15th flight test and its longest mission to date.

The Starship spacecraft performed its orbital insertion burn and entered Earth's orbit. It later deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites.

After emerging from thick clouds over the Texas coast, the spacecraft reignited three engines, flipped into a vertical position and slowed its descent toward the launch tower. The mechanical arms then successfully caught the spacecraft.

candidates.title: See Jupiter and Mars make a spectacular close approach overnight Nov. 15-16
candidates.raw_excerpt: Heads up stargazers! Mars meets Jupiter for a spectacular rendezvous in the heart of the constellation Leo on the night of Nov. 15-16, and they won't be this close again until July 2029. Jupiter and Mars will appear a little over 1 degree from each other as they rise over the eastern horizon around midnight for viewers in the U.S., as the blue-white light of the main-sequence star Regulus glows below, according to In-The-Sky . It's all a trick of perspective, but spectacular nonetheless. In reality Mars and Jupiter are separated by a gulf of over 368 million miles (592 million kilometers), while the light from Regulus has travelled for some 79 light-years before reaching Earth . The spectacular display occurs just once every 2-2.5 years , when Mars catches up to Jupiter as it plies its more distant orbit, making the pair appear side by side from our Earthly vantage point — an event known to astronomers as an appulse. Jupiter, Mars and Regulus will appear close together on the night of Nov. 15-16. (Image credit: Created by Anthony Wood in Canva.) Both Mars and Jupiter are "superior planets" whose orbits exist beyond that of Earth. As a result their disks always appear full to us through the eyepiece of a telescope, unlike the inner planets Mercury and Venus , which exhibit moon-like phases as they circle the sun . A 6-inch telescope can reveal the wildly differing natures of the solar system worlds. Slew your scope to Jupiter to spot the gargantuan cloud bands (and zones) that ring the gas giant , formed from masses of ammonia and water that travel in different directions through Jupiter's hydrogen and helium atmosphere, driven by powerful jet streams. The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted a nationwide ground stop on Friday evening after hours of disruption affected thousands of flights across the country. Flight cancellations and delays are expected to continue through the weekend.

More than 10,000 flights were disrupted, according to a report by CNBC, which noted that more flight cancellations were expected to extend into Saturday.

The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned, and the second since the aftermath of the September 11, 2001, attacks.

At a press conference Friday evening, Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said that while nothing was completely certain at that point, there were no indications that a cyberattack was responsible.

Duffy, who was also at the press conference, asked Congress for $50 billion in emergency funding to overhaul the nation's aging air traffic control infrastructure.

Eric Heisserer was so impressed by Ted Chiang's "Understand" that he bought himself a collection of the author's short stories. candidates.title: The Microsoft outage China barely felt: A lesson on data sovereignty
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Microsoft's latest failure was global in reach, but not global in impact.

From around 4.17 p.m. UTC on Thursday, the US tech giant's services including Outlook, Teams, Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive and Copilot, were degraded for more than 10 hours. The disruption reached at least 74 countries, with Outlook complaints on Downdetector – a third-party outage-monitoring platform that aggregates user reports – peaking near 140,000. 

The damage was heavily concentrated in the Americas, Europe and Australia. Governments didn't treat it as a purely private-sector issue. Germany's federal cybersecurity authority, BSI, said it was in contact with Microsoft and that "numerous companies" had been cut off from core cloud services. Australia's Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said he had activated a mechanism requiring Microsoft to prioritize the country's recovery, after both the Australian Federal Police and the domestic intelligence agency ASIO confirmed they were hit. Japan's government said its shared administrative IT backbone, GSS, was disrupted forcing some ministries back to phone communication. The Philippines' Supreme Court warned that email responses and online transactions would be delayed.

China sat in a blank space on that map. 

Why China was unfazed 

Multinationals in Shanghai on Microsoft's global platform were hit, as were Chinese exporters whose partners live on Outlook. Some foreign firms and foreign-related personnel in China using the global version were still affected. But the broader country didn't blink.

All preparations to ensure electricity supply during the event have been completed, the company said.

CSG has secured 89 million kilowatt-hours of green electricity in advance, which will ensure that all energy consumed during the event is covered by green energy. Every unit of electricity used at the Shenzhen venues will have a traceable source.

The green electricity will come from two areas, according to Shen Sai, manager of development and comprehensive management at the marketing and customer service department of CSG's Shenzhen Power Supply Bureau.

One part will come from offshore wind farms in Yangjiang, Guangdong Province, while the other will come from wind and solar power bases in the vast deserts, Gobi areas and barren lands of northwest China, Shen said.
